texto: It is almost midnight. You shuffle into the bathroom,
half asleep. And there it is.
A spider, sitting on the rim of the toilet, staring right back at you.
You do what millions of people do.
You give it one quick push, into the bowl, and you flush.
Whoosh. Gone. Problem solved.
But is it? Where does that spider actually go?
Is it dead? And could it ever climb back up, while you are sitting there?
Here is the short answer from spider expert Jerome Rovner.
Flushed spiders usually drown.
But not quickly. It can take an hour or more.
And some spiders can survive underwater for more than a day.
So let's follow this one, all the way down.
You push the handle, the water spins,
and the spider gets pulled into a dark, curving tunnel.
That curve is the trap. A bend in the pipe that always holds water,
so sewer gas cannot come up into your house.
For a spider, it is the biggest water slide on Earth. In total darkness.
With no lifeguard. Seconds later,
it is under your floor, heading for the street.
And here is the first surprise. A lot of spiders
do not sink. Their bodies are covered in tiny
water-repelling hairs that hold a thin silver layer of air.
So the spider can bob on the surface like
a little life jacket, breathing from its own private bubble.
One European spider, the diving bell spider,
lives its whole life underwater, inside a bubble of air held in
silk. Now it is in the sewer.
Cold, dark, and moving.
Imagine falling asleep in your pajamas and waking up in a flooded subway tunnel,
in a city you have never seen.
That is the spider's night. If the current pushes it under,
its air starts to run out. But a spider burns
energy so slowly that drowning takes a long,
long time. That is why so many spiders seem to come
back from the dead.
In two thousand nine, scientists in France dunked marsh wolf spiders
underwater, to see how long they could last.
Most held on for about sixteen hours. A few lasted around forty.
After a while, they stopped moving completely.
They looked dead. But when the researchers laid
them out to dry, they started twitching, and hours later,
they walked away. They had slipped into a kind of coma.
So the spider you flushed might not be dead yet.
But it is very far from
home. So can it climb back up into your toilet?
The answer is almost certainly no.
It would have to swim back against the flow, through the water in the trap,
and up a slippery porcelain wall.
Spider experts at the Burke Museum know of no proven case of a spider getting
into a house through the pipes.
And the spider you find in your bathtub in the morning? It did not come up the drain.
It climbed down, looking for a drink of water.
And then it could not climb back out of the slippery tub.
And here is the twist.
That spider on your toilet was probably not an intruder
from outside. Many house spiders spend their entire
lives indoors, in quiet corners, eating flies,
gnats and even mosquitoes.
It was not breaking in. It lived there. You just met it for the first time.
And to send it away, you used about a gallon and
a half of clean water. Roughly what you drink in two or three
days. So what should you do next time?
Grab a cup and a piece of paper.
Put the cup over the spider, slide the paper underneath, and carry it out.
A garage or a porch is perfect.
Many house spiders struggle out in the open cold.
Or, honestly, just let it be. It is one more hunter in the house,
working the night shift for free.
So the next time you meet a spider on the toilet at midnight, remember where the
flush really sends it. Not into thin air.
Into a long, dark water slide, and a very bad night.
A cup and a piece of paper.
That is all it takes.
